variants.intertext: The piece of tablet now numbered Israel Museum 55-2 was found by a shepherd in 1954 near the dump of the Chicago expedition to Megiddo (Tell al-Mutasallim), which ran from of 1925–39. Petrographical analysis of the fabric of MB Megiddo shows the tablet to be made of a clay that cannot derive from a source closer to Megiddo than the coastal plain between Ashkelon and Sidon (@bib{goren2009provenance}). On these grounds MB Megiddo is unlikely to have been written in Megiddo itself. The text is set down on the clay without much regard for poetic lines, as was often the habit in the west. Only in those few places where the text agrees closely with MB Ur and SB Tablet VII can one determine where the lines of poetry begin and end. The obverse begins with a reminiscence of the heroes’ epic exploits, apparently voiced by Enkidu (obv. 4′–8′?), followed by an assertion that something, evidently the dream, was favourable but, at the same time, hard to interpret (obv. 10′–12′). The tablet continues with Enkidu telling his second dream, in which he finds himself overpowered by a monstrous opponent and led captive to the Netherworld (obv. 12′–18′?). The reverse describes Enkidu’s deathbed agony and the subsequent grief of Gilgameš. The opening lines are very fragmentary. From this analysis of its contents it seems likely that the Megiddo tablet, when complete, covered events from Enkidu’s dream of doom to his expiry, the episodes that mark respectively the beginning and the end of SB Tablet VII. (adapted from @bib{RN117@339–343}).

variants.reconstruction:
%n [u]nakki[s? | ...]
#note: See @bib{RN117@346}: “In neither Levy’s copy nor Westenholz’s is there room at the beginning of the line for the @akk{[u₂-ul]} restored by Landsberger, but on this tablet it is feasible that a negative particle could have ended the preceding line. Landsberger saw in these lines an assertion by Enkidu of his innocence in the matter of felling the cedar, given that in OB Ishchali, as also in the newly recovered conclusion of SB Tablet V, the emphasis is on Gilgameš as the lumberjack. However, it is clear from Enkidu’s address to the door in SB VII that he, as well as Gilgameš, felled cedar. Elucidation of this passage in MB Megiddo will have to await the discovery of new text.”
%n [a]ttā? | inūma | [...]

%n [š]adûša | u ... [... | ša ina?]
#note: See @bib{RN117@346}: “6′–7′. The restorations are made with reference to Gilgameš’s résumé of his exploits with Enkidu, as given several times later on in the SB text (VIII 52–4, X 31–3 // 128–30 // 228–30): @i{ša ninnemdūma nīlû šadû} / @i{niṣbatūma alâ nināru} / @i{nušalpitu Ḫumbaba ša ina qišti erēni ašbu} (Tablet X adds @i{ina nērebēti}(?) @i{ša šadî nidūku nēšī}). Note that the exploits are given here in the correct order, with the slaying of the Bull of Heaven coming after the killing of Ḫumbaba, not before. In comparison with the late text, Megiddo’s @akk{[š]a-du-ša} presents a problem, for it is not a regular accusative. It might be locative, prompting the restoration [@i{nilû}] @i{šadušša}, but such forms are rare in Gilgameš and it is better to assume that in the reporting of the heroes’ first exploit the text was different from the SB version.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@347}: “The cry is likely to be that of Gilgameš, uttered in anguish at the realization of Enkidu’s approaching death. Collation rules out @akk{id-k[e]}.”

%n kīma summi | udamm[im | ...]
#note: See @bib{RN117@347}: “Or @i{summati}(tu)@akk{{mušen}}. Two restorations have been put forward for the verb in this line. The suggestion of @bib{soden1963assyrisch@82, fn. 1}, was @akk{u₂-ta-am-m[i-il]} < @i{ummulu}, ‘to make writhe’. A less improbable restoration is @akk{u₂-ta-am-m[i-im]}, as proposed by Landsberger. The suggestion was that *@i{utammim} was corrupt for @i{idammum}, a view repeated by @i{CAD} S, p. 379, where the many attestations of the stock simile @i{kīma summati damāmu} are collected (p. 380 for @i{kīma summi damāmu}). I have adopted Landsberger’s reading but reject his analysis. It is less mistrustful of the ancient scribe to assume that the verb in question is a correctly spelled intensive II/1 stem of @i{damāmu}.” See also @bib{RN602@410}: “Für @i{udammim} als D-Stamm von @i{damāmu} s. auch @i{Bildersprache} S. 64.”

%n ēṣat | ina mūš[i? | ...]
#note: See @bib{RN117@347}: “The interpretation of the first three signs as a spelling of @i{ēṣat} follows Goetze and Levy. Landsberger emended to @akk{e ṣa-<bi>-it}, ‘möge er nicht halten’, but emendation is unnecessary. Comparable writings of closed syllables C₁@i{a}C₂ with the sequence C₁@i{a}-@i{i}C₂ have been collected by @bib{groneberg1980gebrochenen@157}, who notes the presence of ‘broken orthographies’ in texts of all periods. Another example in a western copy of a Babylonian literary text is @akk{is-sa₃-ku-AT} for @i{issakut} in @i{VAS} XII 194, 56 (Adapa from Amarna).”

%n ašarēd (|) ... [... | ibakki]
#note: See @bib{RN117@347}: “16′–17′. To my eyes the broken sign after @i{ašarēd} is not @sux{l[u₂]} (Landsberger). The phrase @i{ana ibrīšu} recalls the opening couplet of SB VIII: @i{mimmû šēri ina namāri} / @i{Gilgāmeš ibakki ana ibrīšu}, and I have restored accordingly.”
